notes.b: Before you can follow the cell cycle you need to know what is being copied and shared out: the chromosomes. How many a cell has, and how they are arranged, decides whether it is diploid or haploid.
points: A chromosome is one long DNA molecule wound around proteins, carrying many genes (the units of inheritance). There is more on this in Chromosome structure and genes.

Between divisions the chromosomes are long, thin and spread out as chromatin (DNA with its proteins). Before division they coil up (condense) and become short and thick, so they can be seen with the light microscope when stained.

Homologous chromosomes are a pair of chromosomes of the same size and shape, with the same genes at the same positions, one inherited from each parent; the alleles (versions of a gene) on them may differ. Human body cells contain 23 such pairs.
Diploid (2n): a cell or organism with two sets of chromosomes, so that its chromosomes lie in homologous pairs. Human body (somatic) cells are diploid, 2n = 46. The 46 counts chromosomes, not pairs.

Haploid (n): a cell with one set of chromosomes, one chromosome from each homologous pair. Human gametes (sperm and egg cells) are haploid, n = 23. Haploid means one complete set, not half a chromosome.
When two haploid gametes fuse at fertilisation, the zygote (the first cell of the new organism) is diploid again (23 + 23 = 46), so the chromosome number stays the same from generation to generation.
Haploid cells are made by meiosis, a division that halves the chromosome number; mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same. There is more on this in Mitosis and meiosis.
Each species has its own chromosome number: human 2n = 46, the fruit fly Drosophila 2n = 8, the garden pea 2n = 14. The number does not reflect how complex an organism is.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to define haploid and diploid and to give the number for a cell type. State diploid as two sets (2n) and haploid as one set (n), and give 46 for a human body cell and 23 for a gamete, not 23 pairs.

notes.h: The cell cycle: growth, DNA synthesis and division
notes.b: Cells don't just divide and stop: each one lives through a repeating sequence of events called the cell cycle. It shows how a cell prepares for division and then carries it out.
points: The cell cycle is the sequence of events in the life of a cell, from the time it is formed by division until it divides itself into two daughter cells.
It has three main activities, in this order. First, growth: the cell makes new proteins and organelles (the working parts of a cell) and gets bigger.
Second, DNA synthesis: every chromosome is copied, so the cell has two copies of its genetic information to hand out.
Third, division: the nucleus divides so that each new nucleus gets one copy of every chromosome, then the cytoplasm divides to give two cells.
The phase between divisions, when growth and DNA synthesis happen, is interphase. A cell spends most of its life in interphase, about 90% of the cycle, so division is short.
In many human cells grown in the laboratory, one cycle takes about 24 hours.
Interphase is not a resting stage. The cell is very active, carrying out its normal functions as well as preparing to divide.
One cycle, including division, produces two daughter cells, each with the same number and type of chromosomes as the parent cell and genetically identical to it.
notes.tip: If asked what happens to DNA in interphase, say it is copied (replicated). Never call interphase a resting phase, and don't put DNA replication in prophase.

notes.h: Which cells keep cycling, and how the cycle is controlled
notes.b: Not every cell divides at the same pace, and no cell divides without being told it is safe to. Whether a cell cycles depends on its job and on control checks built into the cycle.
points: Some cells leave the cycle once they are specialised and stop dividing, for example most mature nerve cells. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and can't divide.

Other cells divide often throughout life, for example cells of the skin, the lining of the gut and the bone marrow, and in plants the cells at root and shoot tips (meristems, regions where growth happens).

The cycle is controlled. Proteins inside the cell check at several points (checkpoints) that the cell is large enough, that the DNA has been copied correctly and is undamaged, and that the chromosomes are attached correctly before the cell moves on.
Signals from other cells (growth factors, chemical messages) tell a cell whether to divide. There is more on how loss of this control leads to cancer in Cancer.

Diagram: the cell cycle as a circle. Large sector: interphase (cell growth and DNA replication). Small sector: division (mitosis, then cytokinesis). Arrow for direction. Higher Level: also label G1, S, G2 and the four stages of mitosis.
notes.tip: When you draw the cell cycle, make interphase the big sector and division the small one, and add an arrow showing the direction. Higher Level students must also label the sub-stages.

notes.b: Interphase is long and busy, and it has three parts: G1, S and G2. Together they prepare the cell so that division can be quick and accurate.
points: G1 (first growth phase): the cell grows, makes proteins (including the enzymes needed to copy DNA) and organelles, and carries out its normal job.
S (synthesis) phase: DNA replication, so each chromosome now consists of two identical copies called sister chromatids, joined at the centromere (the narrow point where they are held together).

G2 (second growth phase): further growth and more organelles, for example mitochondria. The proteins of the spindle (the fibres that later pull chromosomes apart) are made, and ATP is stored for division.
A cell that stops dividing leaves the cycle from G1 into a non-dividing state (sometimes called G0), for example mature nerve cells.
Throughout interphase the nuclear membrane (envelope) is intact, the nucleolus is visible and the chromosomes are uncoiled as chromatin, so individual chromosomes can't be seen.
notes.tip: Sister chromatids are identical copies of one chromosome, made in S phase; homologous chromosomes are a pair, one from each parent. Don't confuse them.

notes.h: The stages of mitosis (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Mitosis is the division of the nucleus. It runs as one smooth process, but it is split into four stages to make it easier to describe, and each stage has a characteristic look and job.
points: Nuclear division (mitosis) is a continuous process, divided for convenience into four stages in this order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. It is followed by cytokinesis, which is division of the cytoplasm and not a stage of mitosis.

Prophase: the chromosomes condense (shorten and thicken) and become visible, each as two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. The nucleolus disappears, the nuclear membrane breaks down, and spindle fibres (protein tubes called microtubules) begin to form.
In animal cells, two centrioles move to opposite ends (poles) of the cell and the spindle forms between them. Plant cells have no centrioles but still form a spindle.
Metaphase: the chromosomes line up singly on the equator (middle) of the spindle; each is attached by its centromere to spindle fibres from both poles.
Anaphase: the centromeres split and the spindle fibres shorten, pulling the sister chromatids apart to opposite poles, centromere first, which gives a V shape.
Once separated, each chromatid is called a chromosome, so each pole now has a full set of identical chromosomes. Energy for the movement comes from ATP, the cell's energy carrier.

Telophase: the chromosomes reach the poles and uncoil back into chromatin; a nuclear membrane forms around each set; the nucleoli reappear; the spindle breaks down. There are now two nuclei, each genetically identical to the original.

Diagram: the four stages of mitosis in an animal cell, 2n = 4 (one long and one short homologous pair, shaded to show the two parents). Labels: chromosome, sister chromatids, centromere, spindle fibres, centriole, pole, equator, nuclear membrane (breaking down, re-forming), cell membrane, cleavage furrow (end of telophase).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name, describe and draw the stages and to identify a stage from a diagram. Learn the order, and remember that in mitosis chromatids separate while homologous chromosomes don't pair up. Don't mention prometaphase.

notes.h: Identifying stages and the mitotic index (Higher Level only)
notes.b: You can tell which stage a cell is in just by looking at how its chromosomes are arranged under the microscope. Counting dividing cells then tells you how fast a tissue is dividing.
points: In stained cells from a growing root tip (for example onion or garlic) viewed at ×400, most cells are in interphase, seen as a nucleus with no visible chromosomes, because interphase is the longest part of the cycle.
Dividing cells are identified by the arrangement of their chromosomes: condensed and scattered for prophase; in a line across the middle for metaphase.
Two groups moving apart is anaphase; two groups at opposite ends, with new nuclei forming, is telophase.
The mitotic index is the percentage of cells in a sample that are dividing. For example, 24 dividing cells out of 200 gives (24 ÷ 200) × 100 = 12%.
A high mitotic index shows a tissue that is dividing rapidly, such as a root tip or a tumour.
notes.tip: You may be given a micrograph or numbers to interpret. For the mitotic index, divide dividing cells by total cells counted and multiply by 100, and say that a higher value means faster division.

notes.b: After the nucleus has divided, the cell still has to split in two. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, and plant and animal cells do it differently because plant cells have a rigid wall.
points: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm to form two separate daughter cells. It usually starts during late telophase. Organelles such as mitochondria are shared between the two cells.
In animal cells the cell membrane is pulled inwards around the middle of the cell, forming a groove (cleavage furrow) that deepens until the cell pinches into two.
In plant cells the rigid cell wall can't pinch in. Instead, vesicles (small membrane sacs) from the Golgi apparatus collect across the middle of the cell and fuse to form a cell plate.
The cell plate grows outwards to the sides and becomes the new cell membranes and cell wall between the two cells.
Diagram: an animal cell with a cleavage furrow beside a plant cell with a cell plate forming, each labelled.
notes.tip: To distinguish cytokinesis in plant and animal cells, say animal cells form a cleavage furrow and pinch in, while plant cells build a cell plate. Don't say plant cells pinch in.

Having two sets of chromosomes, arranged in homologous pairs.
Having one set of chromosomes, one from each homologous pair.
The sequence of events from the formation of a cell by division until it divides into two daughter cells.
The phase between divisions, when the cell grows and its DNA is replicated.
A point in the cell cycle where proteins check that the cell is ready to move on.
The two identical copies of a chromosome, joined at the centromere after DNA replication.

questions.prompt: Explain the terms haploid and diploid, giving one example of each type of cell in humans.
questions.model: A diploid cell has two sets of chromosomes, arranged in homologous pairs. Human body cells are diploid, 2n = 46, with 23 pairs. A haploid cell has one set of chromosomes, one from each homologous pair. Human gametes, sperm and egg cells, are haploid, n = 23. When two gametes fuse at fertilisation the zygote is diploid again (23 + 23 = 46).

questions.prompt: Describe the events of interphase and of each stage of mitosis in an animal cell.
questions.model: Interphase has three parts. In G1 the cell grows, makes proteins and organelles, and carries out its normal job. In S phase DNA is replicated, so each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere. In G2 the cell grows further, makes more organelles and spindle proteins, and stores ATP. Prophase: the chromosomes condense and become visible, the nucleolus disappears, the nuclear membrane breaks down, the spindle forms and the two centrioles move to opposite poles. Metaphase: the chromosomes line up singly on the equator, each attached by its centromere to spindle fibres from both poles. Anaphase: the centromeres split and the spindle fibres shorten, pulling the sister chromatids to opposite poles. Telophase: the chromosomes reach the poles and uncoil, a nuclear membrane forms around each set, the nucleoli reappear and the spindle breaks down, leaving two genetically identical nuclei. A labelled diagram of one stage can add marks.

questions.prompt: A student counted 300 cells in a stained root tip and found 36 dividing. Calculate the mitotic index, explain why most cells were in interphase, and state how cytokinesis in these cells differs from that in an animal cell.
questions.model: Mitotic index = (36 ÷ 300) × 100 = 12%. Most cells were in interphase because interphase is the longest part of the cycle, about 90% of it, and division is short. In plant cells the rigid cell wall can't pinch in; vesicles from the Golgi apparatus fuse across the middle of the cell to form a cell plate, which grows outwards to become the new cell wall and membranes. In animal cells the cell membrane is pulled inwards to form a cleavage furrow that pinches the cell into two.
